type:
∀ {τ : Type u_2} [inst : Fintype τ] {δ : ℝ},
  0 ≤ δ →
    ∀ {r : Option τ → ℕ},
      (∀ (j : τ), ↑(r none) ≤ δ * ↑(r (some j))) →
        ∀ {d : τ →₀ ℕ}, Finsupp.degree d ≤ r none → Roth.weight (r ∘ some) d ≤ δ
what: An exponent vector of total degree at most the distinguished natural weight has complementary reciprocal-weight sum at most δ when each complementary weight dominates the distinguished one by the given δ ratio.
how: Split the zero distinguished-weight case using Finsupp.degree_eq_zero_iff. Otherwise use div_le_div_iff₀ for coordinate comparisons, Finset.sum_le_sum and Finsupp.degree_eq_sum to obtain weight ≤ δ times degree divided by the distinguished weight, then apply the degree bound.
hypotheses: Nonnegative delta and distinguished weight at most delta times every other weight; derivative order at most distinguished weight. The exact captured parameters and existing ambient types are printed; no additional project-defined structure is captured.
caller_summary: 1 explicit source caller declarations, all in Theta.lean; 1 direct original value consumers. Exact separate lists retained. Entire Theta module proof bodies replay successfully with fresh target name.
mathlib_api_audit: If the distinguished weight is zero, the degree bound forces the exponent vector to vanish, and δ nonnegativity closes the result. Otherwise its positivity and the ratio assumption force positive complementary weights. Compare each reciprocal-weight summand using div_le_div_iff₀ and the ratio bound, sum with Finset.sum_le_sum, identify the exponent degree with Finsupp.degree_eq_sum, and finish using the degree bound. This supplies the row-order weight estimate in index_le_lem6 from the determinant derivative-degree bounds; it is distinct from determinant nonvanishing and the final scalar index inequality.
moral_duplications: This ratio-to-weight estimate supplies derivative-row admissibility in index_le_lem6; mapped_det_ne_zero_aux instead proves determinant nonvanishing, and index_numeric_bound_aux closes a scalar real inequality. These are distinct proof obligations.
